title: Why Do We Brush Our Teeth?

body.heading: Your mouth is a busy city
paragraphs: Right now, your mouth is home to millions of tiny living things called bacteria. Most are harmless neighbors. But some love to build sticky cities on your teeth — and that is where our story starts.
You cannot see them, but you can feel their city in the morning: that fuzzy feeling on your teeth. It has a name.

body.heading: Plaque: the sticky city
paragraphs: The fuzzy film is called plaque — bacteria and their sticky glue, building up on every tooth. The bacteria in plaque eat the same sugar you eat, from food and drinks left on your teeth.
And here is the problem: after their sugar feast, the bacteria make acid. Acid melts tiny holes in teeth. A hole that grows is a cavity — and cavities hurt.

body.heading: Brushing: the daily sweep
paragraphs: A toothbrush is a broom for the city. Brushing sweeps the plaque away before its acid can do much damage — two minutes, morning and night, top, bottom, front, back and the chewing tops.

Toothpaste with fluoride is the armor delivery: fluoride makes the outside of your teeth harder, so acid has a tougher wall to melt. Grown-ups: a pea-sized blob is plenty for kids, and spitting (not swallowing) is the rule.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Run your tongue over your teeth right now. Fuzzy or smooth? That fuzz is plaque — your tongue is a plaque detector!
2. Why do you think dentists say brush at NIGHT especially carefully? (Hint: what are the bacteria doing while you sleep?)

takeaway: Plaque bacteria feast on sugar and make acid that melts holes in teeth; two minutes of brushing, twice a day, sweeps them away while fluoride hardens the walls.
materials: Just this page to read — brushing itself needs a soft toothbrush, fluoride toothpaste and a grown-up's help
supervision: Grown-ups should help or check brushing until at least age 7–8; children cannot reach every tooth surface alone yet.
safetyNotes: Use only a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste for young children; spit, don't swallow.
Never share toothbrushes. Replace brushes every 3–4 months or after illness.
This page is general information, not dental advice — a dentist who knows the child's teeth comes first.
screenFreeExtension: Two-minute brushing challenge: brush together for a full two minutes (a song or a sand timer helps) and check every surface in the mirror.
